name: Moong Dal Chilla
cuisine: North Indian (Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Delhi street stalls; also "moong dal cheela", "moong dal ka chilla", "moonglet" for the thick, fluffy Delhi style, and close to Gujarat's "moong dal pudla")

ingredients.name: Split yellow moong dal (dhuli moong dal), dry
Onion (pyaz/kanda)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ¼ medium onion, very finely chopped (about 3 tbsp)

ingredients.name: Groundnut oil (or any neutral cooking oil)

equipment: Bowl for soaking, and a sieve or colander
Mixer-grinder with a small chutney jar
Flat non-stick tawa or 9–10-inch non-stick pan
Measuring spoons and a measuring cup (normal teaspoons and a steel glass are fine stand-ins)

steps.title: Measure the dal
steps.text: Measure 50 g (¼ cup) split yellow moong dal into a bowl.
steps.visualCue: A small heap of pale-yellow split lentils, no stones or dark specks.
steps.cameraCheck: ¼ cup dal in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Dal poured from the cup into the bowl.
steps.watchOut: Tiny stones or husk bits hidden in the dal; spread it on a plate and pick them out before rinsing, or you will bite grit later.

steps.title: Rinse the dal
steps.text: Cover with water, swirl with your fingers, pour the water off. Repeat 3 times.
steps.tip: Rinsing removes dust and surface starch, so the batter tastes cleaner.
steps.visualCue: The water goes from cloudy to almost clear.
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl with clear rinse water
steps.videoShot: Fingers swirling the dal in water.
steps.watchOut: Pouring the dal down the sink with the water; hold it back with your palm or a sieve.

steps.title: Soak the dal
steps.text: Add 1 cup (250 ml) fresh water and leave it covered.
steps.visualCue: The dal has swelled to about double, and a grain crushes easily between two fingers.
steps.cameraCheck: A soaked grain pressed between your fingers
steps.videoShot: Fingers squashing a soft, soaked lentil.
steps.watchOut: Under-soaked dal still feels hard in the middle and gives a gritty batter that sticks; soak longer, or use warm water and grind longer if short of time. In a hot kitchen, keep it in the fridge after 4 hours so it does not turn sour.

steps.title: Drain the dal
steps.text: Pour the soaked dal into a sieve and let it drip.
steps.visualCue: No standing water around the dal.
steps.cameraCheck: The drained dal in the sieve
steps.watchOut: Leftover soaking water makes the batter too thin to thicken again; drain for a full minute.

steps.title: Prepare the ginger and chilli
steps.text: Peel the ginger (3 g) and break the green chilli (3 g) into 2–3 pieces.
steps.visualCue: A small peeled ginger piece and chilli pieces
steps.cameraCheck: The ginger and chilli on the board
steps.videoShot: A spoon edge scraping the ginger skin off.
steps.watchOut: Ginger skin left on turns the batter slightly bitter; scrape it off with a spoon edge.

steps.title: Load the grinder
steps.text: Put the drained dal, ginger, chilli, ¼ tsp cumin seeds and 2 tbsp (30 ml) water into the small grinder jar.
steps.visualCue: Dal, aromatics and a little water in the jar
steps.watchOut: Too much water now; you can thin the batter later but you cannot thicken it.

steps.title: Grind the batter
steps.text: Grind in short bursts, scraping down the sides once or twice.
steps.visualCue: A thick, pale-yellow, mostly smooth paste with a slight grain when rubbed between fingers.
steps.videoShot: The jar lid lifted to show the paste.
steps.watchOut: Blades spinning without catching; add 1 tbsp water and grind again. Do not run the mixer non-stop, as the motor and batter heat up.

steps.title: Transfer to a bowl
steps.text: Scrape the batter into the mixing bowl.
steps.visualCue: All batter out of the jar
steps.watchOut: Batter stuck under the blades; scrape it out, as it is a good part of your serving.

steps.title: Chop the onion and coriander
steps.text: Very finely chop 30 g onion and 1 tbsp (5 g) coriander leaves.
steps.visualCue: Tiny, even onion pieces and fine green flecks
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped onion and coriander side by side
steps.videoShot: The knife rocking through the onion.
steps.watchOut: Big onion pieces tear the chilla when you spread it; chop smaller, or sprinkle the onion on top after spreading for the crispest chilla.

steps.title: Season the batter
steps.text: Add ¼ tsp salt, a pinch of turmeric, a pinch of hing, the onion and the coriander. Stir well.
steps.visualCue: An evenly yellow batter speckled with white and green
steps.videoShot: A spoon folding in the onion and coriander.
steps.watchOut: Too much hing tastes harsh and bitter; a true pinch is enough.

steps.title: Adjust the thickness
steps.text: Stir in 1–2 tbsp water, a little at a time.
steps.visualCue: Like thick dosa batter: it falls from the ladle in a thick ribbon and slowly settles, not running like water.
steps.videoShot: The ribbon of batter falling back into the bowl.
steps.watchOut: Batter that is too thin makes a lacy, fragile chilla that tears; stir in a spoon of batter from a second small grind, or just cook thicker, smaller chillas.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Put the tawa on medium heat. Add ½ tsp oil and wipe it across with a folded paper towel or onion half.
steps.visualCue: A sprinkle of water sizzles and disappears in 2–3 seconds.
steps.videoShot: Water drops dancing and vanishing on the hot tawa.
steps.watchOut: A smoking tawa; the chilla will drag and brown before it sets. Take it off the heat for 10 seconds and wipe with a damp cloth.

steps.title: Pour and spread the first chilla
steps.text: Pour half the batter (one ladle, about 75 ml) in the centre. Using the back of the ladle, spread it in circles from the centre out to about 7 inches.
steps.visualCue: An even round, thin enough that the tawa shows through in a few spots
steps.cameraCheck: The spread chilla on the tawa
steps.watchOut: Pressing hard so the batter drags and tears; the tawa is too hot, so cool it, sprinkle water, wipe and try again.

steps.title: Add oil around it
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil around the edges and a few drops on top.
steps.visualCue: The oil sizzles at the edges.
steps.videoShot: The spoon drizzling oil around the edge.
steps.watchOut: Pouring too much oil, which makes the chilla greasy and adds calories; measure with a spoon.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Cook on medium heat without touching it.
steps.visualCue: The top turns from glossy to matte, the edges lift and turn golden, and the base slides when nudged.
steps.videoShot: The spatula lifting an edge to show the browned underside.
steps.watchOut: Flipping too early; the chilla breaks and sticks. If the top is still wet and shiny, wait another 30 seconds.

steps.title: Flip it
steps.text: Slide the spatula under the chilla and turn it over.
steps.visualCue: The cooked side is golden with brown spots.
steps.watchOut: A half-flip that folds the chilla on itself; slide the spatula fully under it and flip in one quick move.

steps.title: Cook the second side
steps.text: Press lightly with the spatula and cook.
steps.visualCue: Light-brown spots and no raw, sticky patches when pressed
steps.cameraCheck: The second side, lifted with the spatula
steps.watchOut: A raw, doughy centre; if it still looks wet when lifted, cook 30 seconds more on low heat.

steps.title: Plate it
steps.text: Fold in half or serve flat on a plate.
steps.cameraCheck: The finished chilla on the plate
steps.videoShot: The chilla sliding onto the plate.
steps.watchOut: Stacking hot chillas flat; they steam and go soft, so plate them side by side or fold them.

steps.title: Make the second chilla
steps.text: Stir the batter, wipe the tawa, and repeat steps 13 to 18 with the remaining batter and the last 1 tsp oil.
steps.visualCue: Two golden chillas on the plate
steps.videoShot: The second chilla joining the first.
steps.watchOut: Batter that has settled and thickened; stir it and add a teaspoon of water if needed. Wipe the tawa clean so crumbs do not burn.

reasons: 50 g moong dal gives about 12.6 g of plant protein and 5.6 g of fibre, with very little natural fat, and the dish is shallow-cooked in 2 tsp oil. It is vegan and dairy-free, and moong is widely regarded as an easy-to-digest dal. Points come off because protein is modest for a full meal, vegetables are few, and sodium is about 600 mg. Restaurant versions are often brushed with butter, made thick and heavy ("moonglet"), stuffed with paneer or cheese, and served with sweet chutneys.

researchRating.basis: moong dal chilla is a widely loved everyday North Indian breakfast and a staple of high-protein, weight-loss breakfast lists. Recipe pages score very high: Hebbar's Kitchen 4.99/5 from 266 votes (re-confirmed this cycle in a search snippet; its Kannada page shows 5 from 14 votes). Cycle 1 figures for Indian Healthy Recipes (5/5, 45 votes), Piping Pot Curry (4.93/5, 13 votes), Tarla Dalal (5/5, 8 reviews) and Spice Up The Curry (5/5, 4 votes) could not be re-checked this cycle (sites unreachable). Small deductions: the soaking step puts some people off, the plain version is seen as everyday rather than a treat, and plain versions are rare on Mumbai delivery menus.

storage: Cooked chillas are best fresh; they go limp as they cool. Leftover chillas keep in an airtight box in the fridge for up to 1 day. Uncooked batter keeps in a closed box in the fridge for up to 2 days (stir in 1–2 tbsp water before using; leave the onion out if storing, and add it fresh). Freezing cooked chillas is not recommended (they turn soggy); the plain batter (without onion) can be frozen for up to 1 month and thawed overnight in the fridge. Reheat on a hot tawa for 30–40 seconds per side; avoid the microwave, which makes them rubbery.
leftoverRemix: Chilla "noodle" upma. Roll 2 leftover chillas and slice into thin ribbons. Heat ½ tsp oil, crackle ¼ tsp mustard seeds and a few curry leaves, add 2 tbsp chopped onion and capsicum, then toss in the ribbons with a pinch of salt and ½ tsp lemon juice for 1–2 minutes. Finish with coriander.
burnOff: about 3.7 km of running (260 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 5.2 km of brisk walking (about 1 hour at 5 km/h, about 50 kcal/km) (est.).

navratri.reason: moong dal is a pulse and the recipe has onion and hing; pulses are avoided on the common vrat rule set (common rule set assumed; a samak or singhara-flour pancake is a different dish)

ekadashi.reason: pulses are avoided on Ekadashi in the common rule set (families differ)

jain.reason: drop onion and fresh ginger and use sonth; see Jain variant (powdered turmeric assumed allowed, as in common Jain cooking)

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; light and easy to digest, a good sehri with curd or a side of sprouts since protein is only about 12.6 g (est.)

jain.reason: drop the onion (30 g) and the fresh ginger (3 g, a root); use a pinch of sonth (dry ginger powder) instead (see Jain variant)

vegan.reason: dal, vegetables, spices and groundnut oil only; no dairy, ghee, honey or egg

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian recipe with no meat or egg

sattvik.reason: leave out the onion (30 g) and the hing (it is the onion-like flavour); the recipe has no garlic (see Jain variant, which also covers this)

glutenFree.reason: the dal is gluten-free, but most hing sold in India is compounded with wheat flour; leave the hing out or use a certified gluten-free hing (see Gluten-free variant)

dairyFree.reason: no dairy in the recipe (serve with a non-dairy chutney rather than curd)
